title: How do Chinese tourists perceive tranquillity during the tour?
country: China; Maldives; Vietnam; Russia; USA; Nepal; Norway (destinations exemplified in Tables 3-4 of Chinese tourists' online travel notes; full destination list NR)
setting: mixed (20 subclasses of tourist 'tranquil areas' in 3 classes: natural and original areas - islands, seashore, lakes, forest e.g. Yellowstone, grassland, desert; traditional and local areas - ancient villages/towns, Jiangnan garden; modern building areas - zoo, city park, museum, university campus; Tables 3-4)
design: qualitative (grounded theory: open, axial and selective coding of online travel notes in NVivo 11 with theoretical sampling and saturation test)
sample_n: 148 online travel notes by Chinese tourists (115 coded: Mafengwo 80, Ctrip 32, TripAdvisor 3; 33 for saturation test: Mafengwo 20, Ctrip 13); number of individual tourists NR
exposure: Soundscape as described in travel notes, part of the environmental stimulus: geophony (waves, streams, waterfall, wind, rain), biophony (birds, livestock, insects) and anthrophony (tourists, traffic, tour guides, local songs, chanting, Da Geng gong, yachts, water scooters) by destination type (Table 4); quietness (no noise, fewer tourists, away from city) as a feature of tranquil environments (Section 5.2.2); no acoustic measurement. Reverse: type of leisure activity as antecedent of perceived tranquillity
behaviour_measure: Self-described tourist behaviours and activities coded from travel notes (Table 2): sightseeing; leisure activities (shopping, entertainment, being close to animals, access to natural sounds); special activities (photography); slow-paced leisure such as dazing, listening to music, chatting with tea or coffee, riding bicycle, reading, having a rest (Section 5.3); recommend/revisit intention also coded (Section 5.6)
key_finding: Tourists described being attracted or disturbed by anthrophony (complaints about traffic and other tourists' noise) and were cheerful when describing water and bird sounds (Section 5.2.1). The authors conclude that tranquillity is associated with slow-paced leisure activities (dazing, listening to music, chatting with tea, cycling, reading) preferably in quiet places with fewer people, whereas shopping rarely produced tranquillity, and that such activities should not take place in crowded or noisy places (Sections 5.3, 5.7, 6). Links are qualitative interpretations; some model paths are marked as not proven (dotted lines, Fig. 1).
effect_stats: NR (qualitative; coded categories with note numbers, Table 2)
